MRI is the study of choice to evaluate degree of spinal cord compression and identify myelomalacia
Emergencies: SVC obstruction, spinal cord compression, hypercalcaemia, massive haemoptysis, tracheal obstruction.
Neurological: Neck stiffness, altered mental status, focal neurological deficits (meningeal TB, spinal cord compression).
Presence of complications: Massive haemoptysis, respiratory failure, spinal cord compression, neurological deficits, cardiac tamponade.
Pathologic fractures / spinal cord compression: Focal bone pain, neurologic deficit — Orthopaedic fixation or radiotherapy, continue systemic therapy, immobilise
Autonomic testing – bladder scan, perianal sensation; spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.
Look‑alike conditions: spinal cord compression, poliomyelitis, acute transverse myelitis, severe vitamin B12 deficiency.

qs.q: Which imaging modality is considered the study of choice to evaluate the degree of spinal cord compression and identify myelomalacia in a rheumatoid arthritis patient with neck pain?
qs.e: MRI is the study of choice to evaluate the degree of spinal cord compression and identify myelomalacia. CT scans are more useful to better delineate bony anatomy and for surgical planning.

qs.q: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive gait instability and hyperreflexia in the lower extremities. Which imaging modality is best suited to evaluate the extent of spinal cord compression and detect associated myelomalacia?
qs.e: Magnetic resonance imaging is the modality of choice for visualizing soft tissues, spinal cord compression, and intrinsic cord changes such as myelomalacia. Computed tomography provides superior visualization of bony architecture but lacks adequate soft-tissue contrast for the neural elements.

qs.q: In a patient experiencing acute spinal cord compression due to a plasmacytoma involving the thoracic spine, which emergency neurosurgical or oncological intervention may be required?
qs.e: Decompressive laminectomy, along with radiotherapy and chemotherapy, is part of the management for paraplegia resulting from spinal cord compression. Joint replacement is an orthopedic procedure meant for joint destruction rather than acute spinal cord compromise.

ai.title: Spinal Cord Compression
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Spinal cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency where external pressure damages the cord, causing progressive neurological loss. Prompt recognition, imaging, and decompression are essential to prevent permanent deficit, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: A focal or circumferential force on the spinal cord that impairs conduction, producing motor, sensory, and autonomic deficits. Diagnosis rests on clinical suspicion and imaging, usually MRI.
b: Rapidly progressive weakness or sensory change
Pain that is worse with movement or at rest
Bladder/bowel dysfunction

t.b: Confirms location, extent, and cause of compression; shows cord edema or myelomalacia
Detects bony lesions, fractures, or calcified masses; guides surgical planning
Identifies gross vertebral collapse or pathological fracture when advanced imaging is absent

sections.p: The ASIA (American Spinal Injury Association) impairment scale grades motor and sensory loss; early stages (ASIA D/E) have better prognosis after decompression.
b: ASIA A – complete loss below level
ASIA B – sensory only
ASIA C – some motor function, <50% key muscles ≥3/5
ASIA D – motor function, ≥50% key muscles ≥3/5
ASIA E – normal

sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, the commonest etiologies are metastatic disease, infection, and trauma.
b: Metastatic solid tumours (breast, prostate, lung) – most frequent overall
Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis from TB or pyogenic bacteria
Traumatic fracture‑dislocation (road‑traffic accidents, falls)
HIV‑related opportunistic infections (TB, cryptococcal, bacterial abscess)
Schistosomal granuloma (rare, endemic areas)
Herbal or traditional medicine‑induced epidural haematoma

sections.p: Patients develop a characteristic pattern of pain, motor weakness, sensory level, and autonomic loss that evolves over hours to days.
b: Localized back/neck pain, often nocturnal
Progressive limb weakness, usually distal first
Sensory level (pinprick loss) below the lesion
Hyperreflexia and positive Babinski above the level
Urinary retention or overflow incontinence

sections.p: Imaging confirms compression; basic labs identify infection or coagulopathy; bedside tests assess neurologic function.
b: Full blood count, ESR, CRP – screen for infection
Serum calcium – hypercalcaemia can mimic neurologic signs
HIV test – guides antimicrobial choice

t.b: What is the exact level, cause (tumour, abscess, fracture), and cord signal? – Guides urgent decompression
What is the canal diameter and bony involvement? – Alternative for surgical planning
What is the current functional grade? – Determines urgency and prognosis

sections.p: Unrelieved compression leads to irreversible cord injury, respiratory compromise, and autonomic dysreflexia.
b: Rapidly worsening motor power (≥1 grade in 12 h)
New onset respiratory insufficiency (cervical lesion)
Severe autonomic dysreflexia (hypertensive crisis, bradycardia)
Spinal shock with loss of all reflexes

sections.p: Immediate goals are to stabilise the spine, treat the underlying cause, and decompress the cord surgically or with radiotherapy when surgery is not feasible.
b: Immobilise with rigid cervical collar or spinal board
High‑dose intravenous steroids (e.g., dexamethasone) only if tumour‑related and no infection
Empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics for suspected pyogenic infection (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) while awaiting cultures
Anti‑TB therapy (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) for confirmed spinal TB
Urgent decompressive laminectomy or vertebrectomy when surgical capacity exists
Radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours when surgery unavailable

sections.p: After decompression, monitor neurologic recovery, manage pain, and address the primary disease to avoid recurrence.
b: Repeat MRI at 4–6 weeks to assess decompression adequacy
Physiotherapy for gait and strength retraining
Bone health optimisation (calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonates) in metastatic disease
Adherence to anti‑TB regimen for at least 9 months

sections.p: Several conditions produce similar motor‑sensory patterns but differ in etiology and management.
b: Acute transverse myelitis – inflammatory, often post‑viral, no mass effect on imaging
Severe vitamin B12 deficiency – subacute, dorsal column signs, reversible with supplementation
Cauda equina syndrome – lower‑lumbar root compression, saddle anesthesia, early surgical decompression

sections.p: Certain investigations may appear normal despite serious compression.
b: Plain X‑ray may miss early epidural tumour or small abscess
Normal ESR does not exclude TB in HIV‑positive patients
Negative blood cultures do not rule out spinal infection if antibiotics already given

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive weakness or paralysis within hours
Severe neck or back pain with neurologic change

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over CT?
faq.a: MRI shows soft‑tissue detail, cord edema, and tumour extent without radiation, which CT cannot.

faq.q: Can steroids be given in all cases?
faq.a: Only when compression is tumour‑related and infection is excluded; steroids worsen infections.

faq.q: What is the first step if MRI is unavailable?
faq.a: Stabilise the spine, obtain a CT scan, and start empiric antibiotics if infection is likely.

exam: What immediate bedside actions do you take for a patient with suspected cervical cord compression? — Immobilise, assess ASIA grade, arrange urgent imaging, start steroids only if tumour is likely.

How does spinal TB present differently from metastatic compression? — TB often has constitutional symptoms, subacute pain, and vertebral collapse; metastasis is usually painless and associated with known primary cancer.
Which imaging modality confirms cord edema and why is this important? — MRI with T2‑weighted sequences shows myelomalacia, indicating irreversible injury if delayed.
What are the contraindications to high‑dose dexamethasone in this setting? — Active infection (especially TB), uncontrolled diabetes, and recent gastrointestinal bleed.

How would you differentiate cauda equina syndrome from lumbar cord compression clinically? — Cauda equina has saddle anesthesia, absent anal wink, and early bowel/bladder loss; lumbar cord compression shows a sensory level and upper motor signs.

In a resource‑limited hospital without radiotherapy, how do you manage a radiosensitive metastatic lesion? — Prioritise surgical decompression if feasible; otherwise use high‑dose steroids and systemic chemotherapy if appropriate.
What laboratory tests help distinguish pyogenic from tuberculous spinal infection? — Elevated CRP and neutrophilia suggest pyogenic; high ESR, lymphocytosis, and positive TB PCR support TB.
Why is autonomic dysreflexia a red flag in cervical compression? — It can cause life‑threatening hypertension and bradycardia, requiring immediate blood pressure control.
